automata.title: Finite Automata
automata.description: Study deterministic and non-deterministic finite automata. Build DFAs and NFAs, convert regular grammars, and step through input words.
automata.overviewText: Finite Automata are the simplest computational models used to recognize patterns. They consist of states, transitions, and accept/reject decisions. DFAs and NFAs form the foundation for lexical analysis, pattern matching, and regular expression engines.
automata.concept1Desc: Build either type — the editor flags non-determinism in your transition table.
automata.concept2Desc: Paste a right-linear regular grammar and convert it to an NFA in one click.
automata.dfaPoint2: Exactly one active state at any time
automata.nfaPoint2: Set of active states explored in parallel
automata.feature1: Build DFAs and NFAs visually using a transition table
automata.feature2: Convert a right-linear regular grammar into an automaton
automata.feature3: Step through an input word and watch the state diagram update
automata.feature4: Batch-test multiple words and inspect accept/reject results
automata.exercise1Desc: Create a DFA that accepts strings ending in '01'
automata.exercise2Desc: Design an NFA for a given regular expression

number.title: Number Systems
number.description: Master conversions between Binary, Octal, Decimal, and Hexadecimal. Understand IEEE 754 floating-point representation.
number.overviewText: Number systems are fundamental to how computers store and process data. Understanding binary, octal, and hexadecimal representations is essential for low-level programming, networking, and digital design.
number.ex_u03_binAddDesc: Convert two decimal numbers to binary and add them.
number.ex_u04_binToHexOctDesc: Convert 8-bit binary numbers to hex and octal.
number.ex_u05_floatToBinDesc: Convert simple floating point numbers to binary.
number.ex_u05_ieeeEncodeDesc: Convert float values to the 32-bit IEEE 754 standard.
number.ex_u05_ieeeDecodeDesc: Calculate the decimal value of an IEEE 754 32-bit string.
number.examplesFallback: Interactive examples for Number Systems will be available here.
number.example_u03_1_desc: Convert the decimal number 26 to binary.
number.example_u03_2_desc: Add the numbers 50 and 13 as binary numbers.

number.example_u04_2_desc: Represent the binary number 0011 1100 as an octal number.
number.example_u04_3_desc: Represent the octal number 760 as a hexadecimal number.
number.example_u04_4_desc: Represent the hexadecimal number 7F as a binary number.
number.example_u05_1_desc: Convert the decimal number 10.5 to a binary floating point number.
number.example_u05_2_desc: Represent 3.375 as a normalized binary floating point number.

encoding.title: Encoding
encoding.description: Learn Base64 and UTF-8 encoding. Understand how text is converted to Base64 strings and how characters are represented as UTF-8 byte sequences.
encoding.overviewText: Encoding schemes like Base64 and UTF-8 are fundamental to how data is transmitted and stored. Base64 converts binary data to ASCII-safe text, while UTF-8 provides a universal character encoding that supports all writing systems.
encoding.ex_base64_placeholder_desc: Encode a text string to Base64.
encoding.ex_utf8_placeholder_desc: Encode characters to their UTF-8 byte sequence.
encoding.ex_ascii_easy_desc: Convert the character '{{char}}' to its ASCII value (decimal and hex). What is the decimal ASCII value?
encoding.ex_utf8_easy_desc: Convert the Unicode value U+{{hex}} (range 0x0000-0x007F) to its UTF-8 binary representation.
encoding.ex_time_easy_desc: Given the Unix timestamp {{timestamp}}, what is the counter value exactly {{hours}} hours in the future?
encoding.ex_base64_medium_desc: Convert the string '{{str}}' (exactly 3 characters, no padding needed) to Base64.
encoding.ex_utf8_medium_desc: Convert the Unicode value U+{{hex}} (range 0x0800-0xFFFF, requires 3 bytes) to its UTF-8 binary representation.
encoding.ex_time_medium_desc: Person A was born at timestamp {{birthTimestamp}}. Today is timestamp {{nowTimestamp}}. Is the person 18 or older? (Answer: Ja/Nein)
encoding.ex_base64_hard_desc: Decode the Base64 string '{{encoded}}' (with padding ==) back to ASCII text.
encoding.ex_utf8_hard_desc: Which Unicode value (U+XXXX) corresponds to the 3-byte UTF-8 binary sequence '{{binary}}'?
encoding.example_utf8_1_desc: Encode the text 'Hello' to UTF-8 bytes.

moore.title: Moore & Mealy Machines
moore.description: Explore sequential circuit design with Moore and Mealy state machines. Learn the differences and when to apply each model.
moore.overviewText: Moore and Mealy machines are finite state machines with output. In Moore machines, output depends only on the current state. In Mealy machines, output depends on both the current state and the current input. Both are fundamental to digital circuit design.
moore.exercise1Desc: Create a sequence detector as Moore machine
moore.exercise2Desc: Create a sequence detector as Mealy machine
moore.exercise3Desc: Convert a Moore machine to equivalent Mealy
moore.exercise4Desc: Convert a Mealy machine to equivalent Moore

dnf.title: Disjunctive Normal Form
dnf.description: Learn how boolean expressions are evaluated with truth tables and how the Disjunctive Normal Form is derived from the rows with result 1.
dnf.overviewText: Disjunctive Normal Form (DNF) writes a boolean expression as OR-linked AND terms. In the lecture style, each truth-table row with result 1 contributes exactly one term.

algebra.title: Boolean algebra rules
algebra.intro: These rules let you rewrite a DNF into shorter equivalent forms. They power the step-by-step solution path and the worked examples in the simulator.

identity.name: Identity
identity.example: 1 acts as the neutral element of ∧ and 0 as the neutral element of ∨.

domination.name: Domination
domination.example: Whatever is OR-ed with 1 is forced to 1; whatever is AND-ed with 0 is forced to 0.

idempotence.name: Idempotence
idempotence.example: Repeating the same operand neither tightens nor relaxes the term.

double_negation.name: Double negation
double_negation.example: Two negations cancel each other out.

complement.name: Complement
complement.example: A variable is always either true or false — so a ∨ ¬a is always 1, and a ∧ ¬a is always 0.

commutativity.name: Commutativity
commutativity.example: Operand order does not affect the result for ∧ and ∨.

associativity.name: Associativity
associativity.example: With multiple ∧ or ∨ operations, the grouping does not matter — (a ∧ b) ∧ c equals a ∧ (b ∧ c).

distributivity.name: Distributivity
distributivity.example: A shared operand can be factored out — like factoring in regular maths, but with ∧ and ∨ instead of · and +.

absorption.name: Absorption
absorption.example: If a is already true, then a ∨ (a ∧ b) is also true — the AND part adds nothing.

de_morgan.name: De Morgan
de_morgan.example: Negation flips the operator: ∧ becomes ∨ and each operand is negated.

lectureExpression.title: Expression with an AND group
lectureExpression.explanation: The expression is true when a=1 or b and c are both 1.

parentheses.title: Parentheses change the result
parentheses.explanation: Here c=1, and a=1 or b=1 must also hold.

negation.title: Negation restricts the true rows
negation.explanation: Because ¬a is set, only rows with a=0 can be true. Additionally, b or c must equal 1.

xor.title: Half-adder sum as XOR
xor.explanation: The sum is 1 when exactly one input is 1.

carry.title: Half-adder carry
carry.explanation: The carry bit is only 1 when both inputs are 1 — a single AND term.

exercise.walkthroughRowsText: Rows {{rows}} provide the terms of the correct DNF.

exercise.walkthroughFactoredNote: This form is mathematically equivalent but no longer a DNF (the outer operator is ∧). It is only relevant when the shortest boolean expression is asked for, not the shortest DNF.

java.title: Java Programming
java.description: Work with core Java basics such as console output, loops, and arrays. The simulation tab provides a directly editable Java code editor.
java.overviewText: This topic introduces simple Java programs step by step. The focus is on the Main class, the main method, console output, loops, and small array-based tasks.
java.example1Text: The smallest Java program with a main method and a console print statement.
java.example2Text: A for loop is the standard way to repeat the same instruction several times.
java.example3Text: An integer array can be sorted in ascending order with Arrays.sort.
java.exercise1Desc: Write a Java program that prints Hello World to the console exactly once.
java.exercise2Desc: Use a loop to print Hello World to the console exactly five times.
java.exercise3Desc: Add two integer values and print the sum in the console.
java.exercise4Desc: Sort an integer array in ascending order and print the result afterwards.
java.exercise5Desc: Iterate over an array and determine the largest contained value.

commandOverview.title: What works in the Java editor?
commandOverview.versionText: The browser compiler uses OpenJDK javac through teavm-javac. Language diagnostics come from javac; the generated program runs as WebAssembly in a browser worker.
commandOverview.limitationsText: Write one Main.java-style program. You can run Java source code, but you cannot type terminal commands into the editor.

programShape.title: Program entry point
programShape.description: One Main.java program works. public class Main and additional non-public helper classes can be placed in the same editor file.

basics.title: Basic Java syntax
basics.description: Basic Java syntax works: variables, operators, if/else, switch, and method calls.

loops.title: Loops and control flow
loops.description: for, while, do/while, and for-each work for exercises and small algorithms.

arraysCollections.title: Arrays, lists, maps, and sets
arraysCollections.description: Arrays and typical java.util collections work: Arrays.sort, ArrayList, LinkedList, HashMap, HashSet, Collections.sort.

objects.title: Own types
objects.description: Custom classes, constructors, enums, records, interfaces, and static methods can be placed in the same editor file.

output.title: Console output
output.description: Output is captured and shown in stdout or stderr below the editor.

standardLibrary.title: Standard library subset
standardLibrary.description: Common library classes from java.lang, java.util, java.math, and simple java.time are available. OS-facing APIs are not reliable.

singleFile.title: One editor file
singleFile.description: The UI currently sends one source file. Put helper classes into the same file instead of using a multi-file project.

input.title: Console input
input.description: Scanner and System.in work with the input box below the editor. Input is provided before the program starts; interactive prompts during execution are not supported.

cli.title: Terminal commands
cli.description: The editor expects Java source code, not commands. java, javac, jshell, jar, mvn, and gradle are not executed as terminal commands.

environment.title: OS access
environment.description: Local files, sockets, started processes, and native libraries are blocked by the browser runtime model.

runtimeFeatures.title: Dynamic runtime features
runtimeFeatures.description: Reflection-heavy code, dynamic class loading, and real Java threads are not reliable in this WebAssembly target.

stringsMath.title: Strings, Math, and big numbers
stringsMath.description: StringBuilder, String methods, Math functions, BigInteger, and BigDecimal work for typical console tasks.

run.title: Compile and run the current editor content
run.description: The Run button sends the Java source to the browser compiler, generates WebAssembly, and executes the Main.main method in the worker.

compile.title: Compilation is available as part of Run
compile.description: The internal compiler command uses javac diagnostics and TeaVM code generation. The UI does not expose a separate standalone compile-only terminal command.

javaCli.title: No java command-line launcher
javaCli.description: Typing or expecting a local java command is not supported because the browser environment does not start JVM processes.

javacCli.title: No javac terminal command
javacCli.description: javac is embedded inside the browser compiler pipeline. Users cannot pass arbitrary javac flags or compile multiple project files from a local directory.

jshell.title: No interactive JShell
jshell.description: The simulator executes complete programs with a Main class. It does not provide a REPL or interactive command prompt.

tools.title: No packaging or documentation tools
tools.description: Tools such as jar, javadoc, Maven, Gradle, and other local executables are outside the supported browser compiler workflow.

stdin.title: Console input is not interactive
stdin.description: Console output through System.out and System.err is supported. Scanner/System.in uses the fixed simulator input box.

environment.title: Browser sandbox restrictions apply
environment.description: Programs should avoid local files, sockets, native libraries, process execution, and environment-dependent APIs because WebAssembly runs inside a browser worker.

addition.desc: Positional addition in binary. Adding two ones creates a carry to the next position.

addition.overflowWarning: Overflow error! The addition of logically positive numbers resulted in a negative two's complement result.

subtraction.desc: Binary subtraction is usually performed as addition with the negative number (in two's complement).
subtraction.step3: 3. Add the two's complement to Number A
subtraction.carryOutInfo: Since we subtract via two's complement, a carry-out usually means the result is positive. We just discard the carry in this fixed-point system.

multiplication.stepDesc: Bit {{n}} ({{bit}}) = 1, so multiplicand {{val}} shifted left by {{shift}} = {{result}}

division.desc: Written division by trial (go from left to right).
division.stepDesc: Step {{n}}: {{current}} >= {{divisor}}, so 1 to quotient and subtract {{divisor}}

shifting.desc: Here you can shift binary numbers to the left or right.
shifting.shiftLeftExpl: A left shift by n positions corresponds to a multiplication by 2^n.
shifting.shiftRightExpl: A right shift by n positions corresponds to a division by 2^n (without remainder).
shifting.leftStepsTitle: Left Shift: Zeros are appended on the right
shifting.rightStepsTitle: Right Shift: Bits fall off on the right
shifting.stepLeftShift: Bits shift left. A {{count}} zero is appended.
shifting.stepRightComplete: All {{count}} right bits have been removed.
shifting.stepRightZero: Shift by {{count}} >= length of number, result is 0.

ieee754.desc: Addition of two 32-bit floating-point numbers according to IEEE 754.
ieee754.shiftBitDesc: Shift {{n}}: Bit moved to the right.
ieee754.mantissaShifted: The mantissa of the smaller number is shifted to the right by {{diff}} places.
ieee754.expAligned: Now both operands have the exponent 2^{{exp}} and can be added (or subtracted).
ieee754.normBack: The result is converted back into the format 1.M × 2^E.
ieee754.shiftDesc: The mantissa of the smaller number is shifted to the right by {{diff}} places.
ieee754.addDesc: Now both operands have the exponent 2^{{exp}} and can be added.
ieee754.normDesc: The result is converted back into the format 1.M × 2^E.

compare.desc: Compares two binary numbers bit by bit from left to right.
compare.pad: The numbers are padded to the same length (with zeros on the left).
compare.resultEq: The numbers are equal in size.
compare.resultGreater: Number A is greater than Number B.
compare.resultLess: Number A is less than Number B.
compare.padDesc: The numbers are padded to the same length (with leading zeros):
compare.stepEqual: Position {{pos}}: Both bits are {{bit}}, continue to next bit.
compare.stepResultGreater: At position {{pos}}: A has 1, B has 0 → A is greater than B.
compare.stepResultLess: At position {{pos}}: A has 0, B has 1 → A is less than B.
compare.finalResultNote: Since a difference was found here, the comparison is complete. Further bits are no longer considered.

numbers.sameBase: Input and target base are identical.
numbers.lockedDesc: Click the button to show the result and calculation steps.
numbers.enterValue: Enter a number to see the calculation steps.
numbers.decToBinDesc: The number is continuously divided by base 2. The remainders, read from bottom to top, give the binary number.
numbers.divByBaseDesc: The number is continuously divided by base {{base}}. The remainders, read from bottom to top, give the result.
numbers.binToDecDesc: Each digit is multiplied by the corresponding power of base 2 and added.
numbers.otherToDecDesc: The conversion works analogously with the sum of powers to the given base.
numbers.invalidRange: Please enter a value between -128 and +127.

numbers.biasDesc: The IEEE 754 standard adds a bias of 127 to the actual exponent to store negative exponents without a sign.
numbers.mantissaDesc: The mantissa stores the decimal places after normalization.
numbers.hiddenBitDesc: Because normalization ensures there is always a 1 before the comma (except for 0), this 1 is not stored to save 1 bit of space.

topic.title: Turing Machines
topic.description: Learn about the fundamentals of computation through Turing Machines and their transition functions. Explore the limits of what can be computed.

overview.overviewText: A Turing Machine is a mathematical model of computation that defines an abstract machine which manipulates symbols on a strip of tape according to a table of rules. It provides a simple yet powerful framework for understanding what problems can be solved algorithmically.

exercises.exerciseWorksheetAlternatingSymbolsDesc: Given a binary word over {0, 1}, construct a Turing machine that checks whether 0 and 1 always alternate, halting as soon as two equal symbols follow each other or the end of the input is reached.
exercises.exerciseWorksheetSwapFirstTwoSymbolsDesc: Construct a Turing machine that swaps the first two input symbols, leaves all remaining symbols unchanged, and finishes on the third symbol.
exercises.exerciseWorksheetSetFirstAndLastToOne: Set First and Last Symbol to 1
exercises.exerciseWorksheetSetFirstAndLastToOneDes: Construct a Turing machine that overwrites the first and last input symbols with 1, leaves all other symbols unchanged, and finishes on the last input symbol.
exercises.exerciseWorksheetAlternatingOverwriteDes: Construct a Turing machine that overwrites the input from left to right with alternating 0 and 1 symbols and finishes on the last input symbol.
exercises.exerciseWorksheetOverwriteLastTwoWithZer: Set the Last Two Symbols to 0
Construct a Turing machine that overwrites the last two input symbols with 0 and finishes on the last input symbol.
exercises.exerciseWorksheetAsciiParityBitDesc: Given an input of exactly seven bits, construct a Turing machine that counts the number of ones, writes the even-parity bit to the blank cell left of the input, and finishes on the first blank cell after the input.
exercises.exerciseEraseTapeDesc: Build a machine that replaces the whole input word with blanks and halts once the tape is cleared.
exercises.exerciseInvertBinaryWordDesc: Build a machine that flips every 0 to 1 and every 1 to 0, then halts on the first blank cell.
exercises.exerciseUnaryIncrementDesc: Build a machine that appends one additional 1 to the end of a unary word and then halts.
exercises.exerciseDuplicateZerosDesc: Construct a Turing machine that doubles the number of 0s on the tape when they are enclosed by two 1s. Examples: 101 -> 1001, 1001 -> 100001.
exercises.exerciseAddBinaryDesc: Construct a Turing machine that is able to add two numbers in binary representation. To simplify the task, you may make assumptions. For example, you may define that the first addend (the left one) is greater than the second addend, that the read head always starts on the first input symbol, or that a specific symbol must appear between the numbers.
exercises.exerciseCheckRegexDesc: Given the regular expression R1 = (1(01)* | 0(10)*) construct a Turing machine that checks whether an arbitrary binary word can be described by R1. After execution, the tape must contain either a 't' for true or an 'f' for false. Example: The input 11001 cannot be represented by R1, so the tape contains an 'f' and everything else has been removed.
exercises.exerciseBinaryIncrementDesc: Build a machine that adds 1 to a binary number on the tape and halts with the incremented result.

examples.example1Desc: A complete machine that inverts every bit in a binary word while scanning from left to right.
examples.example2Desc: A compact machine that scans to the end of a unary word and writes one extra 1.
examples.example3Desc: A carry-based machine that increments a binary word by one.
examples.example4Desc: A complete binary-adder machine for inputs such as 101+11. Follow the tape states and transitions to see how the second addend is consumed and the result is built.
examples.example5Desc: Search for two consecutive zeros and then write E. Example: The input ⋄1001⋄ produces the output ⋄100E⋄.
examples.example6Desc: The tape contains a finite sequence of 0s and 1s bounded by ⋄ on both sides. Search for three consecutive zeros, write E after them, and halt. The head then rests on the symbol to the left of E. If the pattern is not found, the machine stops on ⋄. Example: ⋄10000⋄ becomes ⋄1000E⋄.
examples.example7Desc: Under the same conditions, search for the pattern 010, write E after it, and halt with the head on the symbol to the left of E. Example: ⋄10100⋄ becomes ⋄1010E⋄. The inputs 0010 and 00010 also contain the pattern.

buildFromScratch.title: Build Your Own Automaton
buildFromScratch.description: Start with a blank canvas and create your own DFA or NFA from scratch. Add states, define the alphabet, and build transitions step by step.
buildFromScratch.hint: You can switch between DFA and NFA mode at any time in the editor.

examplesTab.title: Predefined Examples
examplesTab.subtitle: Learn how finite automata work by studying these examples. Each one includes a step-by-step explanation of how and why it was built.

exercisesTab.title: Practice Exercises
exercisesTab.subtitle: Build each automaton yourself. Use hints if you get stuck — full solutions only if you ask.

endsWith01.title: Strings ending with "01"
endsWith01.goal: Build a DFA that accepts binary strings ending with "01".
endsWith01.description: Design a DFA over {0, 1} that accepts exactly those strings whose last two symbols are "0" followed by "1" (e.g. "01", "101", "1001"). Strings ending in any other pattern must be rejected.
endsWith01.hint1: Track how much of the pattern "01" you have matched so far. Three states are enough: nothing, just saw a 0, just saw "01".
endsWith01.hint2: From the accept state, reading a 0 should fall back to "just saw a 0" (you might still be on track), and reading a 1 should reset to "nothing".

endsWith00.title: Strings ending with "00"
endsWith00.goal: Build a DFA that accepts binary strings ending with two zeros.
endsWith00.description: Design a DFA over {0, 1} that accepts exactly those strings whose last two symbols are both 0 (e.g. "00", "100", "1100"). Single zeros or strings ending in 1 must be rejected.
endsWith00.hint1: You need to remember how many trailing zeros you have just seen. Three states (0, 1, or 2 trailing zeros) are enough.
endsWith00.hint2: From the "two trailing zeros" state, reading another 0 should stay there, but reading a 1 should jump back to "zero trailing zeros".

evenOnes.title: Even number of 1s
evenOnes.goal: Accept binary strings containing an even number of 1s (including zero 1s).
evenOnes.description: Design a DFA that tracks the parity of 1s seen so far. The empty string should be accepted (zero is even).
evenOnes.hint1: You only need two states — one for "even" and one for "odd".
evenOnes.hint2: Reading 0 never changes the parity, but reading 1 always flips it.

noConsecOnes.title: No two consecutive 1s
noConsecOnes.goal: Accept binary strings that never contain "11" as a substring.
noConsecOnes.description: Design a DFA that rejects any string in which two 1s appear next to each other. Strings like "0", "01", "010" are accepted; "11", "0110" are rejected.
noConsecOnes.hint1: Track whether the last symbol you read was a 1. Reading another 1 immediately after must lead to a dead state.
noConsecOnes.hint2: A dead (trap) state has self-loops on every symbol and is not accepting.

divBy3.title: Binary numbers divisible by 3
divBy3.goal: Accept binary strings whose decimal value is divisible by 3.
divBy3.description: Build a DFA that tracks the running remainder of the binary value modulo 3. Accept the states representing remainder 0.
divBy3.hint1: You only need three states — one for each possible remainder (0, 1, 2).
divBy3.hint2: When you are in state with remainder r and read bit b, the new remainder is (2·r + b) mod 3.
divBy3.hint3: The start state and the single accept state are both the same: remainder 0.

grammarTwoOnesZeros.title: Automaton from Grammar: 11 0ⁿ
grammarTwoOnesZeros.goal: Build a DFA for the language L = { 11 0ⁿ | n ≥ 0 }: two ones followed by any number of zeros.
grammarTwoOnesZeros.description: Given the right-linear grammar S → "1" A, A → "1" B, B → "0" B | ε, build the corresponding finite automaton and then check whether the word "11001" belongs to the language.
grammarTwoOnesZeros.hint1: After the two required ones, only zeros may follow — another one leads to a trap state.
grammarTwoOnesZeros.hint2: You need three useful states (start, after the first 1, after the second 1 = accept state) plus a trap state. The word "11001" ends in the trap state and therefore is not in the language.

grammarOnes.title: Automaton from Grammar: 1 0ⁿ 1
grammarOnes.goal: Build a DFA for the language generated by the grammar below.
grammarOnes.description: Construct a DFA that accepts exactly the words derived by this right-linear grammar. Each non-terminal becomes a state; the ε-production marks an accepting state.
grammarOnes.hint1: Create one state per non-terminal (START, A, B) plus a trap state for invalid input.
grammarOnes.hint2: ε at B means that B is accepting; direct every undefined transition to the trap state.

grammar0011.title: Automaton from Grammar: (0011)⁺
grammar0011.goal: Build a DFA for the language generated by the grammar below.
grammar0011.description: Construct a DFA that accepts exactly the words derived by this right-linear grammar. Each non-terminal becomes a state; the ε-production marks an accepting state.
grammar0011.hint1: Chain one state per non-terminal: START→A→B→C→D along the symbols 0, 0, 1, 1.
grammar0011.hint2: D = "0",A jumps back to read another 0011 block, so D's transition on 0 returns to A.
grammar0011.hint3: ε at D makes D the accepting state; every unexpected symbol leads to the trap state.

grammarOnesZero.title: Automaton from Grammar: 1ⁿ 0
grammarOnesZero.goal: Build a DFA for the language generated by the grammar below.
grammarOnesZero.description: Construct a DFA that accepts exactly the words derived by this right-linear grammar. Each non-terminal becomes a state; the ε-production marks an accepting state.
grammarOnesZero.hint1: A = "1",A is a loop on 1; A = "0",B leaves the loop on a 0 and enters the accepting state B.
grammarOnesZero.hint2: B is accepting (ε); every input from B leads to the trap state.

grammarToAutomaton.sectionTitle: Constructing a Finite Automaton from a Regular Grammar
grammarToAutomaton.sectionDescription: Every right-linear grammar defines a language. Open an exercise to build the DFA in the simulator — use the hints and reveal the reference automaton for comparison when needed.

endsWith01.title: Binary strings ending in 01
endsWith01.description: A DFA that accepts all binary strings that end with the substring "01". This is one of the most common introductory DFA examples.
endsWith01.step1: We want to accept exactly those binary strings that end with "01". The automaton must remember whether the last two symbols it read were "0" followed by "1".
endsWith01.step2: We need three states: s0 (start — haven't seen the start of "01" yet), s1 (just read a "0" — could be the first part of "01"), and s2 (just read "01" — accept state).
endsWith01.step3: From s0: reading "0" moves to s1 (potential start of "01"), reading "1" stays in s0. From s1: reading "1" moves to s2 (we found "01"!), reading "0" stays in s1 (new potential start). From s2: reading "0" moves to s1, reading "1" goes back to s0.
endsWith01.step4: The automaton always tracks how much of the pattern "01" has been matched so far. No matter how long the string is, it only needs 3 states because it only cares about the last two characters. This is the power of finite automata — they can recognize patterns with constant memory.

evenOnes.title: Even number of 1s
evenOnes.description: A DFA that accepts binary strings containing an even number of 1s (including zero 1s). A classic example of parity checking.
evenOnes.step1: We want to accept strings where the count of '1' symbols is even (0, 2, 4, ...). The automaton just needs to track the parity (even or odd) of 1s seen so far — it doesn't need to count them exactly.
evenOnes.step2: Only two states are needed: 'even' (we have seen an even number of 1s) and 'odd' (we have seen an odd number of 1s). The start state is 'even' because zero 1s is even. The accept state is also 'even'.
evenOnes.step3: Reading a '0' never changes the parity, so both states loop back to themselves on '0'. Reading a '1' flips the parity: even→odd and odd→even. That's the entire automaton!

containsAba.title: Contains substring "aba"
containsAba.description: An NFA that accepts any string over {a, b} that contains "aba" as a substring anywhere within it. Demonstrates nondeterminism.
containsAba.step1: We want to accept any string that contains "aba" somewhere inside it. Before and after the pattern, any combination of 'a' and 'b' is allowed.
containsAba.step2: An NFA is natural here because we don't know when "aba" starts. The NFA can "guess" nondeterministically — in state s0, when it reads 'a', it both stays in s0 (in case this isn't the start of the pattern) AND moves to s1 (in case it is). If any path leads to acceptance, the string is accepted.
containsAba.step3: Four states: s0 (haven't started matching), s1 (matched "a"), s2 (matched "ab"), s3 (matched "aba" — accept state, stays here forever on any input).
containsAba.step4: In a DFA, we'd need to carefully track partial matches and overlaps. With the NFA, we simply "try all possibilities" at once. The simulator tracks all active states in parallel, showing how the NFA explores multiple paths simultaneously.

epsilonNfa.title: NFA with ε-transitions
epsilonNfa.description: An NFA that uses epsilon (ε) transitions — transitions that happen without reading any input symbol. Demonstrates spontaneous state changes.
epsilonNfa.step1: An ε-transition allows the automaton to move from one state to another without consuming an input symbol. This means the automaton can be in multiple states simultaneously even before reading any input.
epsilonNfa.step2: Before processing starts, we compute the ε-closure of the start state — all states reachable by following ε-transitions from q0. Here, q0 has an ε-transition to q1, so the initial active states are {q0, q1}.
epsilonNfa.step3: q0 reads 'a's and can spontaneously jump to q1 via ε. q1 reads one 'b' and moves to q2. q2 spontaneously jumps to q3 via ε. q3 is the accept state and accepts any remaining input.
epsilonNfa.step4: ε-transitions make it easier to combine automata (e.g., for union or concatenation of languages). They don't add computational power — every NFA with ε-transitions can be converted to one without — but they make automaton construction more modular and intuitive.

divisibleBy3.title: Binary numbers divisible by 3
divisibleBy3.description: A DFA that accepts binary numbers whose decimal value is divisible by 3. An elegant example showing how automata can perform arithmetic.
divisibleBy3.step1: We want to accept binary strings that represent numbers divisible by 3 (remainder 0 when divided by 3). For example: "0" (0), "11" (3), "110" (6), "1001" (9) should all be accepted.
divisibleBy3.step2: When reading a binary number left-to-right, each new bit doubles the current value and adds the new bit. So if the current value is V and we read bit b, the new value is 2V + b. We only care about V mod 3, which has just 3 possible values: 0, 1, or 2.
divisibleBy3.step3: Three states represent the three possible remainders: s0 (remainder 0 — accept state), s1 (remainder 1), s2 (remainder 2). The start state is s0 because we start with value 0, which has remainder 0.
divisibleBy3.step4: For each state (remainder r) and input bit b: new remainder = (2r + b) mod 3. For example: from s1 reading '0': (2×1+0) mod 3 = 2 → go to s2. From s1 reading '1': (2×1+1) mod 3 = 0 → go to s0. This mathematical derivation gives us a complete, correct transition table.

lecture.title: Lecture Example
lecture.description: A DFA from the lecture exercise that accepts one or more '0's followed by exactly one '1' (Regex: 0+1).
lecture.step1: The automaton requires at least one '0', followed by exactly one '1', and then nothing else. It rejects empty strings, strings starting with '1', or strings with more than one '1'.
lecture.step2: s0 is the start state. Reading '0' moves to s1 (we have our 0s). From s1, reading '1' moves to s2 (the accept state). Any other input leads to s3, which is a "sink" or "trap" state because the string is invalid.

grammar.title: Grammar → Automat
grammar.description: The right-linear grammar G = {S → 0S | 0A, A → 1A | 1} is converted into an NFA and then into a minimal DFA via subset construction. Both recognize the language L = {0ⁿ 1ᵐ | n,m ≥ 1}.
grammar.step1: Construct a finite automaton for the regular grammar: G = {S → 0S | 0A, A → 1A | 1} over Σ = {0, 1}. This grammar generates '0's then '1's. Each non-terminal becomes a state, and each production becomes a transition.
grammar.step2: Map productions to transitions: (S → 0S) becomes δ(S,0)=S; (S → 0A) becomes δ(S,0)=A. This creates non-determinism at state S on input '0'. The rule (A → 1) implies a transition to a dedicated accept state (sF). Result: A 3-state NFA {S, A, sF}.
grammar.step3:
We group NFA states into sets to ensure one transition per input.
1. Start at q0 = {S}.
2. Move on '0': δ(q0, 0) = {S, A} → new state q1.
3. Move on '1': δ(q0, 1) = ∅ → sink state qD.
4. δ(q1, 0) = {S, A} → loops back to q1.
5. δ(q1, 1) = {A, sF} → new state q2.
6. δ(q2, 0) = ∅ → qD. δ(q2, 1) = {A, sF} → loops back to q2.
q2 is the accept state (contains sF). qD is a dead/trap state.

rl.title: Regular Languages
rl.description: Work with regular languages and their right-linear grammars — enumerate the words generated by a grammar, derive a grammar from a language definition, and test word membership.
rl.overviewText: A regular language is a set of words that can be described by a regular grammar or a finite automaton. This module focuses on right-linear (Type 3) grammars.
rl.concept1Desc: A right-linear (Type 3) grammar has rules of the form A → aB or A → a, optionally A → ε. This makes it equivalent to an NFA.
rl.concept2Desc: A regular language can be specified either as a finite list of words or with set-builder notation such as { a^n c b^m | n, m > 0 }, using exponents and lower bounds.
rl.concept3Desc: Whether a word belongs to L(G) can be decided by simulating the NFA equivalent to the grammar — it is accepted exactly when a derivation consumes the complete word.
rl.feature1: Enumerate the language generated by a grammar up to a maximum word length
rl.feature2: Generate a grammar from a word enumeration or set-builder notation
rl.feature3: Check whether a word belongs to the language generated by a grammar

grammarToLanguage.title: Grammar → Language
grammarToLanguage.description: Enumerates the first words generated by a grammar using breadth-first search over its derivations.
grammarToLanguage.step1: Starting at the start symbol, breadth-first search expands productions and records every accepted prefix up to the selected length limit. Words are returned in length-lexicographic order.

languageToGrammar.title: Word List → Grammar
languageToGrammar.description: Creates a regular grammar from an explicit set such as L = {"ab", "abb", "abbb"} by combining the words into a prefix tree.
languageToGrammar.step1: The set contents consist of comma-separated words, with or without quotation marks. Each word is processed separately.
languageToGrammar.step2: Each unique prefix becomes a new non-terminal. Every tree edge creates a production A → aB, and each word ending marks its corresponding non-terminal as ε-producing.

languageSetBuilder.title: Pattern → Grammar
languageSetBuilder.description: Reads set-builder notation with exponents and conditions and directly derives a right-linear grammar that generates exactly this language.
languageSetBuilder.step1: The pattern is read as a sequence of factors, such as a^n, c, b^m. The conditions determine a lower bound for each variable. The same variable may not occur in two factors because that would not be regular, as in a^n b^n.
languageSetBuilder.step2: Each factor contributes its own production block: a^0 creates a Kleene-star loop, a^≥1 creates a required first symbol followed by a loop, and a^k creates k fixed productions. The blocks are chained so the start symbol derives the complete word.

recognizeWord.title: Recognize a Word
recognizeWord.description: Checks whether a concrete word belongs to the language generated by a grammar.
recognizeWord.step1: The grammar is converted to an NFA. The NFA is simulated symbol by symbol over the input word. The word is accepted if any path reaches a final state after consuming the complete input.

lectureGrammar1.title: Lecture Example
lectureGrammar1.description: Read this right-linear grammar: words begin with at least one 0 and end with exactly one 1.
lectureGrammar1.step1: Every derivation follows S → 0A → 0…0A → 0…01, so each word consists of one or more zeros followed by a single one. Load it to enumerate L = {01, 001, 0001, …}.

lectureGrammar2.title: Exercise 1
lectureGrammar2.description: Read this grammar: strictly alternating zeros and ones, beginning with either symbol, with a minimum length of 1.
lectureGrammar2.step1: The ε-productions on A and B allow the derivation to stop after any symbol, while A and B continue alternating. Load it to enumerate L = {0, 1, 01, 10, 010, 101, 0101, …}.

lectureLanguage1.title: Exercise 2
lectureLanguage1.description: Find a grammar for this language: at least one 0, exactly one 1, followed by at least one 0.
lectureLanguage1.step1: A loop builds the leading zeros, one rule consumes the single 1, and a final loop builds the trailing zeros. Load it to derive S → 0S | 0A, A → 1B, B → 0B | 0.

languageToGrammar.title: Language → Grammar

applied.title: Applied Grammars
applied.description: Model real token formats such as integers and identifiers as regular grammars.

g2lFiniteBinary.title: Three-bit Words
g2lFiniteBinary.description: Enumerate every word that can be derived by this grammar.
g2lFiniteBinary.goal: List the complete finite language L(G).
g2lFiniteBinary.hint1: Every derivation has the form START → 1A → 1xB → 1xy, so every word has exactly three symbols.
g2lFiniteBinary.hint2: A and B each offer 0 or 1 — producing 2 × 2 = 4 words, all beginning with 1.

g2lTrailingZero.title: Ones between Zeros
g2lTrailingZero.description: Determine the language generated by this grammar.
g2lTrailingZero.goal: Describe the infinite language and list its first words.
g2lTrailingZero.hint1: A → 1A repeats and appends ones; the derivation can end only through A → 0B → 00.
g2lTrailingZero.hint2: Every word therefore consists of a leading 0, any number of ones, and then 00.

g2lEpsilonLoop.title: Recursion with ε
g2lEpsilonLoop.description: List the derivable words when B is also allowed to generate the empty word.
g2lEpsilonLoop.goal: Enumerate the shortest words and account for B's ε-production.
g2lEpsilonLoop.hint1: B → ε lets a derivation end immediately after a 1; B → 0A returns to A.
g2lEpsilonLoop.hint2: Words begin with 0 and alternate between blocks of zeros and ones — trace every A/B transition.

g2lGrouped.title: Grouped Alternatives
g2lGrouped.description: Resolve the grouped rules and enumerate the generated language.
g2lGrouped.goal: Read the parentheses as ordinary alternatives and list the words.
g2lGrouped.hint1: The parentheses only group alternatives: A = "0",A | "1",B and B = "1",B | "0".
g2lGrouped.hint2: A adds leading zeros; B adds ones and must end with a single zero.

l2gZeroOnesZero.title: One 0, Some 1s, One 0
l2gZeroOnesZero.description: Find a regular grammar that generates exactly these words.
l2gZeroOnesZero.goal: Write right-linear rules that generate 0 1ⁿ 0 for n ≥ 1.
l2gZeroOnesZero.hint1: Every word is a 0, followed by one or more ones, followed by a final 0.
l2gZeroOnesZero.hint2: Use a state that loops on 1 (B → "1",B) and terminates on the final 0.

l2gFourWords.title: Four Fixed Words
l2gFourWords.description: Write a grammar that derives exactly this finite language.
l2gFourWords.goal: Generate exactly these four 4-bit words and nothing else.
l2gFourWords.hint1: All four words share the suffix 11; only the first two bits vary.
l2gFourWords.hint2: Let START and A freely choose 0 or 1, then enforce B → "1",C and C → "1".

l2gNestedZeros.title: Blocks of Zeros
l2gNestedZeros.description: Construct a grammar that generates this language.
l2gNestedZeros.goal: Generate words of the form 1 0ⁿ 1 0ᵐ 1 with n, m ≥ 1.
l2gNestedZeros.hint1: Every word begins and ends with 1 and has another 1 in the middle.
l2gNestedZeros.hint2: Between the ones are blocks containing one or more zeros — this requires a loop on 0.
l2gNestedZeros.hint3: Chain START→A→B for the first zero block and then →C→D for the second; B and D loop on 0.

appliedIntegers.title: Integers
appliedIntegers.description: Write a grammar for valid integers: an optional minus sign and no leading zeros.
appliedIntegers.goal: Accept 0, 42, -100…, but reject 007 and a minus sign by itself.
appliedIntegers.hint1: Handle "0" as a separate case so a leading zero cannot begin a longer number.
appliedIntegers.hint2: A first nonzero digit (1–9) may be followed by any number of digits (0–9).
appliedIntegers.hint3: Make the state for following digits ε-producing so the number can end at any point.

appliedIdentifiers.title: Identifiers
appliedIdentifiers.description: Write a grammar for variable names: a lowercase first letter followed by uppercase or lowercase letters, with no digits.
appliedIdentifiers.goal: Accept x, foo, myVar…, but reject uppercase letters or digits at the beginning.
appliedIdentifiers.hint1: The first symbol must be a lowercase letter from a–z.
appliedIdentifiers.hint2: Then loop over any letters (a–z or A–Z) and allow ε to terminate.
